title: The Kinds of Flute and Suitable Materials
summary: Names the three kinds of flute (Tripurā, Kṛṣṇā, Jihvāvatī) and ranks materials from iron through copper and silver to wood, with well-seasoned bamboo best. Then the base rule: measure the bore's inner circumference with a paper ring; a tube eight to nine times that is best, and under six times will not make a flute.

blocks.verse:
तेन बंशी तृधा लोके दृश्यते तृगुणात्मिका।
तासाम् नामानि त्रिपुराथ कृष्णा च जिह्वावती।।९।।
blocks.text: Hence the flute is seen in the world in three kinds, resting on the three guṇas; their names are Tripurā, Kṛṣṇā and Jihvāvatī.

Thus three kinds of flute, the gift of three ages and based on the three guṇas, are mainly in use today. Their names are Tripurā (the flute blown from the bamboo's natural opening), Kṛṣṇā (the transverse, side-blown flute) and Jihvāvatī (the fipple flute). Then, on the basis of these, many suṣira vādya (wind instruments), such as the bīn (reed pipe) and the shehnai, are held to have arisen.

blocks.verse:
निर्माणे या विधिस्तासाम् नादशास्त्रेण सम्मता।
लिख्यते साररूपेण लघुबुद्धया विविच्य च।।१०।।
blocks.text: The method of making them that is approved by the science of sound (nāda-śāstra) is written here in essence, after reflection, with [my] small understanding.

The method of making them that accords with the śāstra I am writing down after reflecting on it with my small understanding. Perhaps this process of making will be useful to our flute-playing brothers.

blocks.verse:
योगेश्वरस्य कृष्णस्य प्रेरणा यादृशी भवेत।
मादृशाम् तादृशी बुद्धिर्जनानाम् कर्मवर्त्मनि।।११।।
blocks.text: As the inspiration of Kṛṣṇa, lord of yoga, may be, so is the understanding of people like me on the path of action.

I have no importance in writing this work, because the Lord's inspiration, working through circumstances, gets done by each person whatever work it wants done by them. So first of all I have to consider which metal is how useful for the flute.

blocks.verse:
लौहखण्डात् तु ताम्रम् स्यात् तस्माद्रजत खण्डकम्।
तस्माच्छ्रेष्ठं तु काष्ठं स्यात् सर्वस्माद् बंश खण्डकम्।।१२।।
blocks.text: Copper is better than a piece of iron, and a piece of silver better than that; better than that is wood, and best of all is a piece of bamboo.

In the flute, nādotpatti (the production of sound) comes from the vibration of air, whatever solid casing that air may be enclosed in; even so, with different vessels there is always a subtle difference in the impact of the air. Among metals that conduct electricity, silver [and] aluminium are better than iron [and] copper, because it is good if the instrument is light. And non-conducting materials such as wood are said to be better than these. But bamboo, which produces supporting sounds through its aṇurandhra (micro-pores), is the best of all.

blocks.verse:
यदा बशं सुपक्वं स्यात् तस्य बंशी विशिष्यते।
अणु रन्ध्रेषु नादानाम् स्वयंभूनां च सम्भवात्।।१३।।
blocks.text: When the bamboo is well seasoned, the flute made from it excels, because self-born sounds arise in its micro-pores.

As far as the question of a suitable material for the flute goes, bamboo is the best. But even among bamboos, the better one is the bamboo that has matured (supakva, well seasoned) thoroughly and naturally. For in ripe bamboo, compared with green bamboo, the aṇurandhra (micro-pores), that is the fine fibres, become more distinct, and its capacity for supporting sound is also greater. Now the question is of making the flute.

Today, among flute players, those artists who do not know how to make a flute are unhappy. The problem before them is whom to have a flute made by, one that is true in tune and matches the desired pitch. If I have to play together in some ensemble, all the instruments will have one fixed pitch, and if my flute does not match it, then I shall have to seek the help of a skilled nirmātā (maker) who can make a flute as I want it. This problem can be fully solved only when artists make their own flutes. So now I shall set out the proper rules for making a flute, which by the grace of [my] guru I found after searching for years.

blocks.verse:
अन्तः परिधिमानेन मुखरात् षड्गुणाधिकम्।
नवतो न्यूनमित्येव मायतिः सुपरीक्षिता।।१४।।
blocks.text: By the measure of the inner circumference, a length from the mouth-hole of more than six times and less than nine [times] has been well tested.

First of all I have to fix the parimāṇa (measure) of the length of the bamboo or pipe, which is to be related to its width. So now I am going to do just that, because every person is three and a half hāth (hastas, cubits) tall by his own hand. This is easier with a pipe, because its width is the same throughout; a bamboo is wider at one end. So the width of the bamboo that counts will be the greater one.

So, to measure that width from inside, roll a piece of thick paper like a chhallā (ring) and put it into the pipe, and see that inside it fits the roundness of the pipe exactly and that the two edges of the paper meet; then take it out. As soon as it comes out, the paper will open out into a length, and just this will be taken as the inner width of the pipe (antaḥ paridhimāna, measure of the inner circumference), because I have to find the width of the body of air inside the pipe. Now let the length of the pipe be measured with the length of that paper: if it is from nine times to eight times, [it is] best; from eight to seven times, middling; and from seven to six times, poor. If it is less than even six times, it will not make a flute. Now, what objection can there be if the length is less or more than this regular measure? For that, attend to the following śloka -

blocks.verse:
ततोऽधिके च न्यूने च बंश खंडे प्रकल्पिते।
स्वासमानानुरोधेन मन्द्रतार व्यतिक्रमः।।१५।।
blocks.text: If the piece of bamboo is made longer or shorter than that, then, in proportion to the breath, the lower and upper registers fall out of order.

For a flute it is necessary that a note one saptaka (octave) higher than the note that sounds when the phūṅk (breath) is kept weak will sound when the breath is made strong. And for this one-octave difference to come out exactly on all seven notes, it is possible only if the length of the pipe or bamboo follows the rule given above, not otherwise. To test this I have blown and tried pieces of pipe from the smallest, whose length equalled the antaḥparidhimāna (measure of the inner circumference), up to the largest, which were 16 times that measure. The corrected measure that came out of this was then fixed. In any case, these days it is a problem for most flute players where to buy a tuneful flute. If someone has somehow trained his breath on an out-of-tune flute, then even another, tuneful flute will be out of tune for him.

Now it must be made clear here how the proper length stated for the flute is valid. If you measure the antaḥparidhi (inner circumference), that is the inner girth, of a pipe and cut the pipe to just that length, then the length and width of the air inside it, which has to be set in motion by the breath, will become equal, and it cannot be set in motion by the breath; so only a bare sound (nāda) will arise in it. If its length is made four times, two sounds can be produced by the breath, about an octave apart. Now if a hole is made in the pipe at 5 times the length, two sounds exactly an octave apart can be produced. So it must be accepted that if we need two forms of each of the seven notes, one octave apart from each other by just lessening or increasing the breath, then for this a pipe of eight times will be right. For if one makes a mukharandhra (mouth-hole) in a pipe of eight times and blows, then as the vega (force) of the breath is raised step by step, 4 sounds of this kind are seen to arise: Sa Ṡa Ṗa Ṡa. With skilful blowing one more sound will come, which we can call the G̈a of the ati-tāra saptaka (very high octave). This is the meaning of the following śloka.
